blocks.heading: Two kinds of formula
blocks.text: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound. A molecular formula gives the actual number of each kind of atom in one molecule. Ethene has molecular formula C2H4 and empirical formula CH2. A molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula, but the multiplier is not known from percentage composition alone. Later organic work also distinguishes structural condensed, displayed and skeletal formula representations; those show connectivity or shape in ways an empirical formula does not.

blocks.heading: From composition to empirical formula
blocks.text: Treat percentage data as masses in a 100 g sample. Divide each mass by the element's Ar to obtain moles. Divide every mole value by the smallest. If the ratios are close to whole numbers, round only after considering the precision of the data. If a ratio is close to 1.5, 1.33 or 1.25, multiply all ratios by 2, 3 or 4 respectively. Multiplying only one ratio destroys the relative composition.

blocks.heading: Empirical formula from percentages
blocks.text: A compound contains 40.0% carbon, 6.7% hydrogen and 53.3% oxygen by mass. For 100 g: carbon moles = 40.0 ÷ 12.0 = 3.333; hydrogen moles = 6.7 ÷ 1.0 = 6.700; oxygen moles = 53.3 ÷ 16.0 = 3.331. Divide by 3.331 to obtain approximately 1.00 : 2.01 : 1.00. The simplest ratio is 1 : 2 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH2O. Formulae do not include decimal subscripts.

blocks.heading: From empirical to molecular formula
blocks.text: The empirical-formula mass of CH2O is 12.0 + 2.0 + 16.0 = 30.0. If the molecule has Mr = 180, the multiplier is 180 ÷ 30.0 = 6. The molecular formula is therefore C6H12O6. The multiplier must be a whole number because a molecule contains whole atoms. A non-integral result signals inconsistent data, incorrect relative masses or a wrong empirical formula.

blocks.heading: Using combustion data
blocks.text: Complete combustion converts all carbon in an organic sample to carbon dioxide and all hydrogen to water. If 0.880 g of CO2 forms, n(CO2) = 0.880 ÷ 44.0 = 0.0200 mol, so n(C) = 0.0200 mol. If 0.450 g of water forms, n(H2O) = 0.450 ÷ 18.0 = 0.0250 mol, so n(H) = 2 × 0.0250 = 0.0500 mol. The ratio C:H is 0.0200:0.0500 = 2:5. Any oxygen in the original compound must be found from a mass difference before its mole amount is included.

blocks.heading: Formulae and equations
blocks.text: A correct formula is fixed before an equation is balanced. The empirical formula describes composition; equation coefficients describe reacting amounts. Keeping those roles separate prevents the common error of altering a subscript in order to balance a reaction.

blocks.heading: Consolidation and checks
blocks.text:
Ratios close to simple fractions need careful scaling. If division by the smallest amount gives 1.00:1.50, multiply both values by 2 to obtain 2:3. For 1.00:1.33, multiply all values by 3 to obtain about 3:4. Do not round 1.50 to 2, because that changes the composition. The precision of the measured composition decides how close a ratio must be before it is recognised as a simple fraction.

When the compound contains oxygen, its mass may be measured directly or obtained by difference. Suppose a 1.50 g sample contains 0.600 g carbon and 0.100 g hydrogen. The oxygen mass is 1.50 − 0.600 − 0.100 = 0.800 g. The amounts are C: 0.600 ÷ 12.0 = 0.0500 mol; H: 0.100 ÷ 1.00 = 0.100 mol; O: 0.800 ÷ 16.0 = 0.0500 mol. Dividing by 0.0500 gives 1:2:1 and empirical formula CH2O. This subtraction is valid only when the sample is stated to contain those three elements.

The empirical formula cannot by itself distinguish compounds that share the same simplest ratio. CH2O could correspond to CH2O, C2H4O2 or C6H12O6. Mr supplies the multiplier. Conversely, if the calculated multiplier is 2.98, experimental rounding may justify 3; a value such as 2.4 does not. Check the original mole ratios and data rather than forcing a molecular formula.
